lead: A water tank is a concrete box that must hold a liquid without leaking, not just without collapsing. Water pushes sideways on every wall, and the pressure grows with depth. The wall must be strong enough for that push and also tight enough that cracks stay hairline for the life of the tank. You meet this in overhead tanks on apartment roofs, underground sumps, elevated service reservoirs and sewage treatment tanks. Strength alone is not the design aim here: crack control and durability decide the steel.
prereq: You need: serviceability and crack control from Unit 2, detailing rules from Unit 3, and the cantilever bending idea from cantilever retaining walls.

sections.h3: Water pushes sideways, and cracks leak

blocks.text: Water in a tank pushes horizontally on the wall. At depth h below the free surface the pressure is p = γwh. The pressure is zero at the top and largest at the base, so the load diagram is a triangle, never a rectangle. Design each ring of the wall for the pressure at its own level; the base gets the maximum.

blocks.where: p is the horizontal water pressure in kN/m² at depth h; γw is the unit weight of water, taken as 10 kN/m³ in design (9.81 kN/m³ more precisely); h is the depth below the water surface in metres.

blocks.text: A tank is not a beam. A cracked beam still carries its load; a cracked tank leaks, because water passes through a crack a fraction of a millimetre wide. So design has two targets at once: enough steel for strength, and low steel stress with closely spaced small bars so cracks stay narrow. Working stress design is popular for tank walls for exactly this reason — the permissible stress is set low on purpose, not because we distrust limit state theory.

Two load cases matter. Tank full: pressure on walls and base, the case that sizes the hoop or bending steel. Tank empty: soil and ground water pushing in from outside, which matters for underground tanks. An empty underground tank can also float if uplift exceeds its own weight plus overburden.

A circular wall is pushed outwards, and it resists by stretching as a ring. That stretch is hoop tension, a direct pull, not a bending moment. To find it, cut the ring across a diameter and take half the ring, 1 m high, as a free body. Water pushes on the projected area 2r × 1 m with total force p × 2r. Two hoop forces T pull back at the cut. So 2T = 2p r, giving T = p r.
T = p r    and    A<sub>st</sub> = T × 1000 / σ<sub>st</sub>
blocks.where: T is the hoop tension in kN per metre height of wall; p is the water pressure at that level in kN/m²; r is the internal radius in m; Ast is the hoop steel in mm² per metre height; σst is the permissible tensile stress in steel in N/mm²: about 130 for direct tension (hoop tension) and about 150 for bending, for Fe 415; the 150 used in the example is illustrative; the 1000 converts kN to N.

blocks.text: The hoop bars are horizontal rings. They sit near the water face, with adequate cover, because the water face is where a crack would leak, and the outer face carries only minimum steel. Keep the spacing small, roughly 100 to 150 mm, so that even a shrinkage crack stays narrow.

Vertical steel depends on the base joint. If the wall is free at the top and the base joint lets the wall slide, hoop tension alone governs. If the base is rigidly held, the wall also bends vertically near the base and vertical steel must carry that moment. The base slab then takes the water weight and spans between the walls.

sections.h3: Rectangular tanks and the base slab

blocks.text: In a long rectangular tank each wall spans vertically between the base slab and the top. An open-top tank is a vertical cantilever fixed at the base and free at the top. The triangular pressure gives a base moment M = γwh³/6 per metre width. For h = 3 m this is 10 × 27/6 = 45 kNm per metre width. Main steel goes on the water face at the base and on the outer face higher up. Short walls instead act as panels supported on three or four edges, bending in two directions, and then need steel both ways on both faces.

items: Fix the geometry: diameter or plan size, and the water depth.
Compute p = γ<sub>w</sub>h at the base and at each level you are designing.
Find hoop tension per metre height (circular) or the bending moment per metre width (rectangular).
Pick a bar diameter and a spacing that gives the required area with spacing under about 150 mm.
Check the base slab, the uplift case, and the joint details.

blocks.text: Liquid tightness is won in the detailing. Use minimum steel on both faces, bars of 8 to 12 mm, spacing 150 to 200 mm, staggered laps, cover of about 40 to 50 mm on the water face, and a low water-cement ratio with good curing. Put water stops at construction joints. A tank that is strong but badly detailed fails its leak test.

figure.caption: The chain from water depth to bar spacing in a circular tank: the pressure at the base sets the hoop tension, which sets the steel area, which sets the spacing of a chosen bar.

spec.title: Circular tank
spec.aria: Flow from 3 m water depth and 3 m radius to 30 kN per square metre pressure, to 90 kN per metre hoop tension, to 600 square millimetre per metre steel, to 10 mm bars at 130 mm spacing.

examples.question: A circular water tank has an internal diameter of 6 m and holds water 3 m deep. Find the hoop tension per metre height at the base. Design the hoop steel using 150 N/mm² as an illustrative permissible tensile stress for this problem, and 10 mm bars, and state the spacing and the steel provided.
steps: Pressure at the base p = γ<sub>w</sub>h = 10 × 3 = 30 kN/m².
Hoop tension T = p r = 30 × 3 = 90 kN per metre height = 90 000 N per metre height.
Steel area A<sub>st</sub> = T/σ<sub>st</sub> = 90 000/150 = 600 mm² per metre height.
Area of one 10 mm bar = π × 10²/4 = 78.5 mm².
Spacing = 1000 × 78.5/600 = 130.9 mm, so provide 130 mm centres.
Steel provided = 1000 × 78.5/130 = 604 mm² per metre, which is more than 600 mm². Safe.
examples.answer: Hoop tension at the base is 90 kN per metre height; the hoop steel is 600 mm² per metre, provided as 10 mm bars at 130 mm centres (604 mm²/m).
examples.check:
import math
gamma_w = 10.0      # kN/m3
D = 6.0             # m
h = 3.0             # m
r = D / 2.0
p = gamma_w * h
T = p * r           # kN per metre height
sigma = 150.0       # N/mm2
Ast = T * 1000.0 / sigma
bar_d = 10.0
ab = math.pi * bar_d**2 / 4.0
spacing = 1000.0 * ab / Ast
spacing_provided = 130.0
Ast_prov = 1000.0 * ab / spacing_provided
print(p)
print(T)
print(Ast)
print(round(spacing, 1))
print(round(Ast_prov, 1))

traps: Using the average pressure for the base hoop tension. With average pressure the answer halves to 45 kN/m, which is wrong; each level uses the pressure at that level.
Putting the diameter into T = p r instead of the radius. That doubles every answer downstream.
Designing only for strength and ignoring crack control. A tank that passes the strength check but has 200 mm spacing and high steel stress will leak.
Unit slips: T comes out in kN per metre, so multiply by 1000 before dividing by N/mm²; and A<sub>st</sub> is mm² per metre height, not the total steel in the wall.

For a rectangular wall with triangular water pressure, using the uniform-load moment p h²/2 instead of γwh³/6. For h = 3 m the correct base moment is 45 kNm per metre; the uniform-load formula gives 30 × 9/2 = 135 kNm per metre, three times too large. Check which load shape you assumed.

quiz.q: What unit weight of water is used in tank design, and what horizontal pressure does 3 m of water create at the base?
quiz.a: γ<sub>w</sub> is about 10 kN/m³ for design (9.81 kN/m³ more precisely). p = γ<sub>w</sub>h = 10 × 3 = 30 kN/m² at the base, zero at the surface.

quiz.q: Why is working stress design common for water-retaining walls?
quiz.a: Because leakage governs as much as strength. A low permissible steel stress, about 130 N/mm² for direct tension (hoop tension) and about 150 N/mm² for bending, for Fe 415, with small bars at close spacing, keeps crack widths small at service loads, so the wall stays liquid tight.

quiz.q: A circular tank has internal radius 4 m and holds water 4 m deep. Find the hoop tension per metre height at the base and the steel needed at a permissible stress of 140 N/mm².
quiz.a: p = 10 × 4 = 40 kN/m². T = p r = 40 × 4 = 160 kN per metre height. A<sub>st</sub> = 160 000/140 = 1143 mm² per metre height.

quiz.q: A rectangular tank wall is 3 m high, open at the top and fixed to the base slab. Find the design moment per metre width at the base.
quiz.a: For triangular pressure, M = γ<sub>w</sub>h³/6 = 10 × 27/6 = 45 kNm per metre width, acting at the base with tension on the water face.

quiz.q: The hoop of a circular tank is in direct tension all round. Why then is the main hoop steel placed near the water face?
quiz.a: The whole section is in tension, so the section needs steel on both faces for crack control. But the crack that leaks is the one that reaches the water face, so the main area is placed there with adequate cover, and the outer face keeps the minimum.

quiz.q: Two tanks hold 3 m of water: a 6 m diameter circular tank and a 3 m high rectangular tank. Why does the circular wall carry the same water so much more cheaply?
quiz.a: The circular wall carries the pressure as hoop tension, a direct pull spread evenly through the section. The rectangular wall must bend as a vertical cantilever, so the same water creates 45 kNm per metre of bending moment, needing a thicker wall and much heavier steel.

quiz.q: Which load case governs an underground tank that may stand empty?
quiz.a: The empty condition with soil and ground water pushing in from outside, together with the uplift check: if the tank's weight plus overburden is less than the upward water force, it can float.

beyond: Not for the exam. Many large circular tanks are prestressed: wire wound round the outside puts the concrete into compression before the water arrives, so the wall never goes into tension and never cracks (see Unit 6). Big tanks are analysed by finite element methods or by standard coefficient tables for walls with different edge conditions. Water stops, pour sequence and curing decide whether a tank passes its leak test as much as the steel does. Search for the Indian standard on liquid-retaining concrete structures, and for 'hoop tension circular tank design'.
